He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse﴾ [of unchastity] ﴿chaste women﴾, meaning the modest ones, ﴿unwary﴾ of immoralities, ﴿believing﴾ in Allah and His Messenger and what he brought from Allah, ﴿are cursed in this world and the Hereafter﴾, meaning: they are removed from the mercy of Allah in this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And for them﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿is a great punishment﴾, and that is the punishment of Hell.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning the chaste women to whom this ruling applies. Some of them said: this applies only to 'Ā'ishah specifically, and it is a ruling from Allah concerning her and concerning whoever accused her, to the exclusion of the rest of the women of the Community of our Prophet ﷺ.

Mention of those who said that:

* Ibn Abi al-Shawarib narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad narrated to us, saying: Khasif narrated to us, saying: I said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Is adultery worse, or the slander of a chaste woman?" He said: "Adultery." I said: "Does not Allah say: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste women...﴾ ... the verse?" Sa'id said: "This was only specifically for 'Ā'ishah."

* Ahmad ibn 'Abdah al-Dabbi narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Awanah narrated to us, from 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah, from his father, who said: 'Ā'ishah said: "I was accused of what I was accused of while I was unaware, and it reached me afterward. Then, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sitting with me, revelation came to him, and when revelation came to him he would be seized as if in a state of stupor. He received revelation while sitting with me, then he sat up wiping his face and said: 'O 'Ā'ishah, rejoice!' I said: 'Praise be to Allah, not to you.' Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unwary, believing women...﴾ ... until he reached: ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾."

Others said: rather, this applies specifically to the wives of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, to the exclusion of other women.

Mention of those who said that:

* It was related to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unwary, believing women...﴾ ... the verse: it refers specifically to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ.

Others said: this verse was revealed concerning 'Ā'ishah, but what is meant by it is everyone who has the description that Allah describes in this verse. They said: this is the ruling for everyone who accuses a chaste woman who has not committed any evil.

Mention of those who said that:

* 'Ali ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: Zayd narrated to us, from Ja'far ibn Burqan, who said: I asked Maymun: "Allah mentioned: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women, then do not produce four witnesses...﴾ ... to His words: ﴿except those who repent after that and reform, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾; He made repentance in that verse, and in the other He said: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unwary women...﴾ ... to His words: ﴿for them is a great punishment﴾." Maymun said: "As for the first, perhaps she has committed something; but as for this one, it is the one who has not committed any of that."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: al-'Awwam ibn Hawshab informed us, from a shaykh of the Banu Asad, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: He explained Surat al-Nur, and when he came to this verse: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unwary, believing women...﴾ ... the verse, he said: "This is concerning 'Ā'ishah and the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, and it is general (mubhamah), and there is no repentance for them." Then he recited: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women, then do not produce four witnesses...﴾ ... to His words: ﴿except those who repent after that and reform...﴾ ... the verse, and said: "So He made repentance for these, and did not make repentance for those who slander those women." He said: Some of the people almost stood up to him and kissed his head, because of the excellence of his explanation of Surat al-Nur.

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unwary, believing women are cursed in this world and the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment﴾ He said: "This is concerning 'Ā'ishah, and whoever does this today against the Muslim women, for him is what Allah said; but 'Ā'ishah was the leader of that."

Others said: this verse was revealed concerning the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, and that was the case until the verse at the beginning of the surah was revealed, which made the lashing obligatory and accepted repentance.

Mention of those who said that:

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to us, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unwary, believing women...﴾ ... to: ﴿a great punishment﴾, meaning the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, whom the hypocrites accused. Allah made cursing, wrath, and returning with the anger of Allah obligatory for them. That was the case concerning the wives of the Prophet ﷺ. Then afterward was revealed: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women, then do not produce four witnesses...﴾ ... to His words: ﴿indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. So Allah revealed the lashing and repentance: repentance is accepted, and testimony is rejected.

The most correct of these opinions in my view is the statement of those who said: this verse was revealed concerning 'Ā'ishah, and its ruling is general for everyone who has the description Allah gave in it.

We say that this is the most correct interpretation because Allah, by His words: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unwary, believing women﴾, encompassed every chaste, unwary, believing woman who is accused of immorality by an accuser, without singling out some over others. So every accuser of a chaste woman with the description Allah mentions in this verse is cursed in this world and the Hereafter, and has a great punishment, unless he repents of that sin before his death. For Allah indicated by His exception in His words: ﴿except those who repent after that and reform﴾ that this is the ruling for the accuser of every chaste woman, whatever the description of the believing chaste woman accused, and that His words: ﴿they are cursed in this world and the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment﴾ mean: this applies to them if they perish without repenting.

The explanation of His words, ﴿On the day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [24:24].

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: And for them there is a great punishment, ﴿on the day when their tongues bear witness against them﴾. The "day" in His words ﴿on the day when they bear witness against them﴾ is connected to His words ﴿and for them there is a great punishment﴾. By His words ﴿on the day when their tongues bear witness against them﴾ is meant the Day of Resurrection, when one of them denies what he earned of sins in this world, when God confronts him with them, so God seals their mouths, and their hands and feet bear witness to what they used to do.

If someone says: How can their tongues bear witness against them when their mouths are sealed? It is said: What is meant is that the tongues of some of them bear witness against others, not that their tongues speak while the mouths have been sealed.

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Amr informed us, from Darraj, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, the disbeliever will be made to recognize his deeds, and he will deny and dispute. It will be said to him: 'These are your neighbours, and they bear witness against you.' He will say: 'They lied.' It will be said: 'Your family and your clan.' He will say: 'They lied.' It will be said: 'Will you swear?' And they will swear. Then God will seal their mouths, and their tongues will bear witness, and then He will admit them into the Fire."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 24, verses 25–26:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On that Day Allah will pay them in full their just due (dinahum al-haqq), and they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth﴾ (25)

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: ﴿On the day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do﴾, Allah will pay them in full their reckoning and their recompense, rightly, for their deeds.

Here, "din" (dīn, recompense/judgment) in this place means the reckoning and the recompense,

as:

⁕ ʿAlī narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allāh narrated to us, saying: Muʿāwiya related to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: ﴿On that Day Allah will pay them in full their just due﴾, he said: "Their reckoning."

The reciters differed over the reading of His saying: ﴿al-ḥaqq﴾. The majority of the reciters of the principal cities read ﴿dīnahum al-ḥaqq﴾ with the accusative (naṣb) as an attribute (naʿt) of "dīn", as if he said: Allah will pay them the reward of their deeds rightly; then the definite article (al-) was added to ḥaqq, so it took the case that dīn took. It is reported from Mujāhid that he read it: "yuwaffīhimu Allāhu dīnahumu al-ḥaqqu" with the nominative (raf') of "al-ḥaqq", as an attribute of Allah.

⁕ Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf narrated this to us, saying: al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, from Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim, from Ḥumayd, from Mujāhid, that he read it "al-ḥaqq" with the nominative. Jarīr said: "And I read it in the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: yuwaffīhimu Allāhu al-ḥaqqu dīnahum."

The correct reading in this matter, in our view, is what the reciters of the principal cities have, namely the accusative of "al-ḥaqq" as following the grammatical case of "dīn", because the consensus of the authorities (ijmāʿ al-ḥujja) is upon it.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth﴾

He says: And they will know on that Day that Allah is the Truth, who makes clear to them the realities of what He used to threaten them with in the world of punishment, and doubt about it will then depart from the people of hypocrisy, who used to doubt what He threatened them with in the world.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men for corrupt words; and good words are for good men, and good men for good words. Those are cleared of what they say; for them is forgiveness and a noble provision﴾ (26)

The commentators differed over the interpretation of this. Some said: its meaning is: corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt words, and good words are for good men, and good men are for good words.

Those who said this:

⁕ Muḥammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men for corrupt words﴾, he said: corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt words.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and good words are for good men﴾

He says: good words are for good men, and good men are for good words. It was revealed concerning those who said about the wife of the Prophet ﷺ what they said of slander. And it is said: "the corrupt for the corrupt": corrupt deeds are for the corrupt, and good deeds are for the good.

⁕ Ibn Bashshār narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from ʿUthmān ibn al-Aswad, from Mujāhid: corrupt speech is for corrupt people, and good speech is for good people.

⁕ Ibn Bashshār narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, the like of it.

⁕ Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, regarding the saying of Allah: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men for corrupt words, and good words are for good men, and good men for good words﴾, he said: "The good words": the good speech, which comes out of the disbeliever and the believer, is for the believer; and "the corrupt words": the corrupt speech which comes out of the believer and the disbeliever, is for the disbeliever. ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾, because He cleared both of what is not true of speech.

⁕ Ḥārith narrated to me, saying: al-Ḥasan narrated to us, saying: Warqāʾ narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding His saying: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men for corrupt words, and good words are for good men, and good men for good words﴾, he said: the corrupt and good words: bad speech and good speech; good for the believers and bad for the disbelievers. ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾, because what the disbelievers say of a good word belongs to the believers, and what the believers say of a corrupt word belongs to the disbelievers, each cleared of what is not true of speech.

⁕ Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men﴾, he said: corrupt speech is for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt speech.

⁕ al-Ḥasan narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, the like of it.

⁕ I was told from al-Ḥusayn, who said: I heard Abū Muʿādh say: ʿUbayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Ḍaḥḥāk say regarding His saying: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men﴾ ... the verse, he said: corrupt speech is for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt speech, and good speech is for good men, and good men are for good speech. This refers to speech; and those who said to ʿĀʾisha what they said, they are the corrupt, and the good are those cleared of what the corrupt said.

⁕ Abū Zurʿa narrated to us, saying: Abū Nuʿaym narrated to us, saying: Salama, that is Ibn Nubayṭ al-Ashjaʿī, narrated to us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men﴾, he said: corrupt speech is for corrupt men, and good speech is for good men.

⁕ He said: Qabīṣa narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ and ʿUthmān ibn al-Aswad, from Mujāhid: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men for corrupt words, and good words are for good men, and good men for good words﴾, he said: corrupt speech is for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt speech, and good speech is for good men, and good men are for good speech.

⁕ He said: Sufyān narrated to us, from Khuṣayf, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men for corrupt words, and good words are for good men, and good men for good words﴾, he said: corrupt speech is for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt speech, and good speech is for good men, and good men are for good speech.

He said: Muḥammad ibn Bakr ibn Muqaddam narrated to me, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd informed us, from ʿAbd al-Malik, that is Ibn Abī Sulaymān, from al-Qāsim ibn Abī Bazza, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Mujāhid: ﴿And corrupt men for corrupt words﴾, he said: corrupt speech is for corrupt men.

⁕ He said: ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd al-Narsī narrated to us, saying: Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatāda: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men for corrupt words, and good words are for good men, and good men for good words﴾, he says: corrupt speech and deed are for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt speech and deed.

⁕ Ibn Wakīʿ narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Ṭalḥa ibn ʿAmr, from ʿAṭāʾ, who said: "The good words for good men, and good men for good words": good speech is for good men, and good men are for good speech, and corrupt speech is for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt speech.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: corrupt women are for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt women.

Those who said this:

⁕ Yūnus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men for corrupt words, and good words are for good men, and good men for good words﴾, he said: it was revealed concerning ʿĀʾisha when the hypocrite cast slander and falsehood upon her, and Allah cleared her of that. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy was the corrupt one, and he was more deserving that the corrupt woman be his and he hers; and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was good, and he was more deserving that the good woman be his; and ʿĀʾisha was the good woman, and she was more deserving that the good man be hers. ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾, he said: here ʿĀʾisha was cleared.

The most preferable of these sayings in the interpretation of the verse is the saying of the one who said: by "the corrupt words" is meant the corrupt words, that is its ugly and bad speech, for the corrupt men and women; and corrupt men among people are for corrupt words, they are more deserving of it because they are its people. And good words, that is its beautiful and fine speech, for good men among people; and good men among people are for good words, because they are its people and more worthy of it.

We only said that this saying is more preferable as the interpretation of the verse because the verses before it came with Allah's rebuke of those who spoke the slander about ʿĀʾisha, and those who accused the chaste, heedless, believing women, and their announcement of what He singled them out with for their falsehood. So concluding the report about the more deserving of the two parties to the slander, the accuser and the accused, is more fitting than a report about others.

* *

And His saying: ﴿Those are cleared﴾

He says: The good men among people are cleared of corrupt speech; if they utter it, Allah pardons them for it and forgives it for them; and if it is said about them, it harms the one who says it and does not harm them. Just as if a good word were said by a corrupt man, Allah would not benefit him by it, because Allah does not accept it; and if it were said to him, it would harm him, because its shame reaches him in this world and its humiliation in the Hereafter.

as:

⁕ al-Ḥasan narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid: ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾, whoever is good is cleared of every corrupt speech; he says: Allah forgives it. And whoever is corrupt is cleared of every righteous speech; Allah returns it to him and does not accept it from him. It has been said: by His saying ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾ is meant ʿĀʾisha and Ṣafwān ibn al-Muʿaṭṭal, the one she was accused with. According to this view, "Those" (ulāʾika) is said in the plural, while the intended meaning is the two of them, as it is said: ﴿And if they are brothers﴾ while the intended meaning is two brothers.

* *

And His saying: ﴿for them is forgiveness﴾

He says: for these good men among people is forgiveness from Allah for their sins, and the corrupt speech if it was from them; ﴿and a noble provision﴾, he says: and for them also, along with forgiveness, is a noble gift from Allah, and that is Paradise, and the honour prepared for them therein.

as:

⁕ Abū Zurʿa narrated to us, saying: al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd al-Narsī narrated to us, saying: Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatāda: ﴿for them is forgiveness and a noble provision﴾: forgiveness for their sins and a noble provision in Paradise.

⁕ Abū Zurʿa narrated to us, saying: Abū Nuʿaym narrated to us, saying: Salama, that is Ibn Nubayṭ al-Ashjaʿī, narrated to us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men﴾, he said: corrupt speech is for corrupt men, and good speech is for good men.

⁕ He said: Qabīṣa narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ and ʿUthmān ibn al-Aswad, from Mujāhid: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men for corrupt words, and good words are for good men, and good men for good words﴾, he said: corrupt speech is for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt speech, and good speech is for good men, and good men are for good speech.

⁕ He said: Sufyān narrated to us, from Khuṣayf, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men for corrupt words, and good words are for good men, and good men for good words﴾, he said: corrupt speech is for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt speech, and good speech is for good men, and good men are for good speech.

He said: Muḥammad ibn Bakr ibn Muqaddam narrated to me, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd informed us, from ʿAbd al-Malik, that is Ibn Abī Sulaymān, from al-Qāsim ibn Abī Bazza, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Mujāhid: ﴿And corrupt men for corrupt words﴾, he said: corrupt speech is for corrupt men.

⁕ He said: ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd al-Narsī narrated to us, saying: Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatāda: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men for corrupt words, and good words are for good men, and good men for good words﴾, he says: corrupt speech and deed are for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt speech and deed.

⁕ Ibn Wakīʿ narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Ṭalḥa ibn ʿAmr, from ʿAṭāʾ, who said: "The good words for good men, and good men for good words": good speech is for good men, and good men are for good speech, and corrupt speech is for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt speech.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: corrupt women are for corrupt men, and corrupt men are for corrupt women.

Those who said this:

⁕ Yūnus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿The corrupt words are for corrupt men, and corrupt men for corrupt words, and good words are for good men, and good men for good words﴾, he said: it was revealed concerning ʿĀʾisha when the hypocrite cast slander and falsehood upon her, and Allah cleared her of that. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy was the corrupt one, and he was more deserving that the corrupt woman be his and he hers; and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was good, and he was more deserving that the good woman be his; and ʿĀʾisha was the good woman, and she was more deserving that the good man be hers. ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾, he said: here ʿĀʾisha was cleared.

The most preferable of these sayings in the interpretation of the verse is the saying of the one who said: by "the corrupt words" is meant the corrupt words, that is its ugly and bad speech, for the corrupt men and women; and corrupt men among people are for corrupt words, they are more deserving of it because they are its people. And good words, that is its beautiful and fine speech, for good men among people; and good men among people are for good words, because they are its people and more worthy of it.

We only said that this saying is more preferable as the interpretation of the verse because the verses before it came with Allah's rebuke of those who spoke the slander about ʿĀʾisha, and those who accused the chaste, heedless, believing women, and their announcement of what He singled them out with for their falsehood. So concluding the report about the more deserving of the two parties to the slander, the accuser and the accused, is more fitting than a report about others.

* *

And His saying: ﴿Those are cleared﴾

He says: The good men among people are cleared of corrupt speech; if they utter it, Allah pardons them for it and forgives it for them; and if it is said about them, it harms the one who says it and does not harm them. Just as if a good word were said by a corrupt man, Allah would not benefit him by it, because Allah does not accept it; and if it were said to him, it would harm him, because its shame reaches him in this world and its humiliation in the Hereafter.

as:

⁕ al-Ḥasan narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid: ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾, whoever is good is cleared of every corrupt speech; he says: Allah forgives it. And whoever is corrupt is cleared of every righteous speech; Allah returns it to him and does not accept it from him. It has been said: by His saying ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾ is meant ʿĀʾisha and Ṣafwān ibn al-Muʿaṭṭal, the one she was accused with. According to this view, "Those" (ulāʾika) is said in the plural, while the intended meaning is the two of them, as it is said: ﴿And if they are brothers﴾ while the intended meaning is two brothers.

* *

And His saying: ﴿for them is forgiveness﴾

He says: for these good men among people is forgiveness from Allah for their sins, and the corrupt speech if it was from them; ﴿and a noble provision﴾, he says: and for them also, along with forgiveness, is a noble gift from Allah, and that is Paradise, and the honour prepared for them therein.

as:

⁕ Abū Zurʿa narrated to us, saying: al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd al-Narsī narrated to us, saying: Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatāda: ﴿for them is forgiveness and a noble provision﴾: forgiveness for their sins and a noble provision in Paradise.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 27:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your houses until you have asked permission and greeted their occupants. That is best for you; perhaps you will be reminded.﴾

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding this. Some of them said: its interpretation is, "O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your houses until you have asked permission."

Mention of those who said this:

Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Hushaym related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he used to recite: "Do not enter houses other than your houses until you seek permission and greet their occupants." He said: "Rather it is 'tasta'nisu' (until you seek to be familiar)," and they were scribes.

Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far related to us, saying: Shu'bah related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning this verse, "Do not enter houses other than your houses until you seek familiarity and greet their occupants," and he said: "It is only an error of the scribe: 'until you seek permission and greet.'"

Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Wahb ibn Jarir related to us, saying: Shu'bah related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, with the like of it, except that he said: "It is only 'until you seek permission,' but it fell out from the scribe."

Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn 'Atiyyah related to us, saying: Mu'adh ibn Sulayman related to us, from Ja'far ibn Iyas, from Sa'id, from Ibn 'Abbas, "until you seek familiarity and greet their occupants," he said: "The scribe erred." Ibn 'Abbas used to recite "until you seek permission and greet," and he would recite it according to the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abu 'Amir related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from al-A'mash, that he used to recite it: "until you seek permission and greet." Sufyan said: "And it has reached me that Ibn 'Abbas used to recite it: 'until you seek permission and greet,' and he said: 'It is an error of the scribe.'"

Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to us, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, his statement: "O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your houses until you seek familiarity and greet their occupants." He said: "Al-istí'nas is al-istí'dhan (seeking permission)."

Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hushaym related to me, saying: Mughirah informed us, from Ibrahim, who said: In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "until you greet its occupants and seek permission."

He said: Hushaym related to us, saying: Ja'far ibn Iyas informed us, from Sa'id, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he used to recite it: "O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your houses until you greet their occupants and seek permission." He said: "Rather it is 'tasta'nisu' (seek to be familiar), and they were of the scribes."

He said: Hushaym related to us, saying Mughirah said, Mujahid said: Ibn 'Umar came from a need, and the sand had harmed him, so he came to the tent of a woman from Quraysh and said: "As-salamu 'alaykum, may I enter?" She said: "Enter with peace." He repeated, and she repeated, while he shifted his weight between his feet. He said: "Say, 'Enter.'" She said: "Enter," and he entered.

He said: Hushaym related to us, saying: Mansur informed us, from Ibn Sirin; and Yunus ibn 'Ubayd informed us, from 'Amr ibn Sa'id al-Thaqafi, that a man asked permission to enter upon the Prophet ﷺ, and said: "Shall I enter, or shall I say 'anlij'?" The Prophet ﷺ said to a slave-girl of his called Rawdah: "Get up to this man and speak with him, for he does not know how to seek permission properly. Say to him: He says, 'As-salamu 'alaykum, may I enter?'" The man heard her, and said it, and he said: "Enter."

Al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to us, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said, concerning His words, "until you seek familiarity," that it is seeking permission. Then it was abrogated and an exception was made: "There is no sin upon you in entering houses not inhabited."

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih related to us, saying: Abu Hamzah related to us, from al-Mughirah, from Ibrahim, concerning His words, "Do not enter houses other than your houses," that he said: "Until you greet their occupants and seek permission."

Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning "until you seek familiarity": "until you seek permission and greet."

Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Ash'ath ibn Sawwar informed us, from Kurdus, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "It is incumbent upon you to seek permission before your mothers and your sisters." Ash'ath said, from 'Adi ibn Thabit: that a woman of the Ansar said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am in my house in a state in which I do not like anyone to see me, whether father or child, and a man of my family keeps entering upon me while I am in that state?" He said: Then there was revealed: "O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your houses until you seek familiarity and greet their occupants..." to the end of the verse.

Others said: The meaning of that is: until you make the people of the house aware (tu'nisu) with coughing, clearing the throat, and the like, so that they know you intend to enter upon them.

Mention of those who said this:

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Hakkam related to us, from 'Anbasah, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, from Mujahid, concerning His words, "Do not enter houses other than your houses until you seek familiarity and greet their occupants," that he said: "Until you cough and clear your throats."

Al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the saying of God, "until you seek familiarity," that he said: "Until you make noise (tajarrasu) and greet."

Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, his statement: "until you seek familiarity," he said: "Cough and clear your throats."

He said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I heard 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah report from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Three verses have been denied by people. God says: 'Indeed the most noble of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you.'" He said: "And they say: 'Indeed the most noble of them in the sight of God is the greatest in rank.'" He said: "And the entire matter of permission has been denied by people." So I said to him: "Should I seek permission before my sisters, who are orphans in my care and live with me in one house?" He said: "Yes." I replied to him that he might grant me a concession, but he refused; so I replied to whoever was present, and he refused. He said: "Would you like to see her naked?" I said: "No." He said: "Then seek permission." I went back to him again, and he said: "Would you like to obey God?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then seek permission." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said to me: "You keep returning to him." I said: "I wanted him to grant me a concession."

Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn Tawus informed me, from his father, who said: "There is no woman more hateful to me that I should see" — as if he meant "her nakedness, or naked" — "from among those who are not mahram." He used to be strict in this.

Ibn Jurayj said, and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: "And when the children among you reach puberty, let them seek permission." So it is obligatory upon all people, when they have reached puberty, to seek permission before whoever among the people (is there). I said to 'Ata': "Is it obligatory upon a man to seek permission before his mother and whoever is behind her of his close kin?" He said: "Yes." I said: "Is it a matter of piety or obligation?" He said: his words: "And when the children among you reach puberty, let them seek permission."

Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn Ziyad informed me that Safwan, a freedman of the Banu Zuhrah, informed him, from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, that a man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Shall I seek permission before my mother?" He said: "Yes." He said: "She has no servant but me; shall I seek permission before her every time I enter?" He said: "Would you like to see her naked?" The man said: "No." He said: "Then seek permission before her."

Ibn Jurayj said, from al-Zuhri: He said: I heard Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil al-Awdi, the blind, that he heard Ibn Mas'ud say: "It is incumbent upon you to seek permission before your mothers."

Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to 'Ata': "Should a man seek permission before his wife?" He said: "No."

Al-Husayn related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Hazim related to us, from al-A'mash, from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Yahya ibn al-Jazzar, from the nephew of Zaynab, wife of Ibn Mas'ud, from Zaynab, who said: When 'Abd Allah came from a need and reached the door, he would cough and spit, out of dislike that he should suddenly come upon us in something he disliked.

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, concerning the saying of God: "O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your houses until you seek familiarity": "Al-istí'nas is tanahhunh and tajarrus, until they know that someone has come to them." He said: "And tajarrus is his speech and his clearing of the throat."

The correct statement regarding this, in my view, is to say: al-istí'nas is the form istif'al from al-uns (familiarity), namely that the people of the house be asked permission to enter upon them, informing those within whether anyone is present, and so that he notifies them that he is entering upon them; so he becomes familiar with their permission to him in this, and they become familiar with his asking permission of them.

It has been related from the Arabs by report: "Go and seek familiarity: do you see anyone in the house?" meaning: "Look, do you see anyone in it?"

So the meaning of the speech, then, when this is its meaning, is: "O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your houses until you greet and seek permission," and that is that one of you says: "As-salamu 'alaykum, may I enter?" And this is of the advanced (muqaddam) which means the delayed; it is in fact "until you greet and seek permission," as we have mentioned from the narration from Ibn 'Abbas.

* *

As for His words: ﴿That is best for you﴾

He says: your seeking familiarity and your greeting the people of the house you intend to enter — that is, your entering it is better for you, because you do not know, if you enter it without permission, what you will fall upon: something that will grieve you or something that will gladden you. But if you enter with permission, you will not have entered upon what you dislike, and by that you will also have fulfilled God's right upon you regarding seeking permission and greeting.

* *

As for His words: ﴿Perhaps you will be reminded﴾

He says: that by your doing that you may be reminded of God's commands upon you and what is binding on you of His obedience, so that you obey Him.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 28:

Discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then if you find no one in them, do not enter them until permission is given to you. And if it is said to you, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: If you do not find in the houses where you seek permission anyone who gives you permission to enter them, then do not enter them, for they are not yours, and it is not lawful for you to enter them except with the permission of their owners. If their owners give you permission to enter them, then enter. ﴿And if it is said to you, "Go back," then go back﴾ means: and if the people of the houses where you seek permission say to you, "Go back, do not enter, and withdraw from them without entering." ﴿It is purer for you﴾ means: your turning back from them when you are told "Go back" and are not given permission to enter them is more pure for you in the sight of Allah.

* *

As for His words, ﴿it﴾:

It refers to the verbal noun derived from the verb [[By "the verbal noun" he means the infinitive (maṣdar), since it is the noun of the action, and he does not mean what the grammarians have conventionally called "verb-nouns" (ism al-fi'l), such as ṣah and uff.]], namely from His words: ﴿go back﴾.

* *

As for His words: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾

He, may His praise be exalted, says: And Allah is aware of what you do, of your going back after seeking permission to enter the houses of others when you are told "Go back," and of your not returning from them, and of your obedience to Allah in what He has commanded and forbidden you regarding that and other matters of His command and prohibition. He has comprehensive knowledge of all of that, counting all of it against you, so that He may recompense you for all of that.

Mujahid used to say about the interpretation of this:

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿Then if you find no one in them﴾ he said: If there is no property of yours in them, then do not enter them without permission. ﴿And if it is said to you, "Go back," then go back.﴾

Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

[Al-Tabari] said: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Hashim ibn al-Qasim al-Muzani narrated to us, from Qatada, who said: A man from the Muhajirun said: I sought this verse my whole life and did not attain it: that I ask permission to enter upon one of my brothers, and he says to me, "Go back," so I go back, and I am glad, because of His words, ﴿And if it is said to you, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you.﴾

This interpretation which Mujahid gave of His words, ﴿Then if you find no one in them﴾, meaning: if there is no property of yours in them, is a distant understanding from the sense of Arabic speech, because the Arabs hardly say, "There is no one in such-and-such a place," except that they mean there is no human being in it. As for goods and all other things other than human beings, and whatever is similar to them, they do not say that about them.

The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 29:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, wherein is provision for you. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: There is no sin or wrongdoing upon you, O people, in entering houses that have no occupant, without seeking permission.

Then they differed about which houses were meant. Some of them said: it means the caravanserais (khans) and the houses built along the roads that have no known occupants, but were built for travellers and wayfarers to take shelter in, and to store their belongings there.

Mention of those who said this:

Yaqub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym told us, saying: Hajjaj informed us, from Salim al-Makki, from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, regarding His words: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited﴾, he said: They are the caravanserais that are on the roads.

Abbas ibn Muhammad narrated to me, saying: Muslim told us, saying: Umar ibn Furrukh told us, saying: I heard Qatada say: ﴿houses not inhabited﴾, he said: They are the caravanserais that are for the people of journeys.

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Za'ida told us, from Warqa', from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, wherein is provision for you﴾, he said: They used to place in houses on the roads of Madina provisions and saddle-frames, so they were given permission to enter them.

Al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿houses not inhabited﴾, he said: They are the houses where travellers lodge, which no one inhabits.

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim told us, saying: Isa told us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan told us, saying: Warqa' told us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, his saying: ﴿houses not inhabited﴾, he said: They used to make or place on the road of Madina saddle-frames and goods in houses in which there was no one, so it was made lawful for them to enter them without permission.

Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan told us, saying: Warqa' told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it, except that he said: They used to place on the road of Madina, without doubt.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it, except that he said: They used to place on the road of Madina saddle-frames and goods.

It was narrated to me from al-Husayn, saying: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His words: ﴿that you enter houses not inhabited﴾: they are the houses that have no people, and they are the houses on the roads and the ruined ones, ﴿wherein is provision﴾, a benefit for the traveller in winter and summer, who takes shelter in them.

Others said: They are the houses of Makka.

Mention of those who said this:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam ibn Salm told us, from Sa'id ibn Sa'iq, from al-Hajjaj ibn Artat, from Salim ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, regarding: ﴿houses not inhabited﴾, he said: They are the houses of Makka.

Others said: They are the ruined houses, and the provision that Allah mentioned in them for you is relieving oneself, by urinating and defecating in them.

Mention of those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I heard Ata' say: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, wherein is provision for you﴾, he said: The relieving of oneself and urination.

Muhammad ibn Umara narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Isa ibn Zayd told us, from his father, regarding this verse: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, wherein is provision for you﴾, he said: Relieving oneself in ruins.

Others said: Rather, it refers to the houses of merchants, in which are the goods of people.

Mention of those who said this:

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, wherein is provision for you﴾: They are the houses of merchants; there is no blame upon you for entering them without permission, the shops that are in the markets and bazaars. And he recited ﴿wherein is provision for you﴾, provision for the people and for the children of Adam.

The most correct of these opinions, in our view, is to say: Allah, by His words ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, wherein is provision for you﴾, encompassed every house that has no occupant, in which there is provision for us, which we may enter without permission. This is because permission is only given to make the one seeking permission feel at ease before entering, or for the one being admitted to be given leave if the house has an owner or occupant. As for a house that has no owner and no occupant, there is no need for permission to enter it, and there is no occupant for whom the one entering needs to be made at ease or greeted, lest he surprise someone of whom he would not wish to be seen. Hence there is no sense in seeking permission there. When that is so, there is no basis for restricting this to some of them and not others. So every house that has no owner and no occupant, whether a house built on some roads for passers-by and wayfarers so that they may take shelter in it, or a ruined house whose people have perished and no one lives in it, wherever that may be, the one who wishes to enter it may enter without seeking permission, for goods of his that he shelters there, or to make use of it to fulfil a need such as urinating, defecating, or other things. As for the houses of merchants, no one may enter them except with the permission of their owners and occupants.

If someone supposes that when a merchant opens his shop and sits for the people, he has thereby given permission to whoever wishes to enter upon him, then the matter is contrary to what he supposes. That is because no one may enter the property of another without a necessity that compels him to do so, or without a cause that makes entry lawful for him, except with the permission of its owner, especially if it contains goods. And if the merchant is known to have opened his shop as permission for whoever wishes to enter, then that too returns to what we have said: that no one entered it except with his permission. Since that is so, the words ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, wherein is provision for you﴾ have no bearing on it, because the houses in which Allah lifted the blame from us for entering without permission are those that are not inhabited; the merchant's shop cannot be entered except with his permission, and it is also inhabited. It is thus clear that it is outside the scope of what Allah intended by this verse.

A group of the people of interpretation said: this verse is an exception from His words: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought familiarity and greeted their occupants﴾.

Mention of those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn Abbas said: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own﴾, then it was abrogated and an exception was made, saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, wherein is provision for you﴾.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih told us, from al-Husayn, from Yazid, from Ikrima, regarding ﴿until you have sought familiarity﴾ ... the verse, that some of it was abrogated and an exception was made, saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, wherein is provision for you﴾.

There is nothing in His words ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, wherein is provision for you﴾ that indicates it is an exception from His words: (Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought familiarity), because His words ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought familiarity and greeted their occupants﴾ are a ruling from Allah concerning houses that have occupants and owners.

And His words ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, wherein is provision for you﴾ are a ruling concerning houses that have no occupants and no known owners. So each of the two rulings concerns a meaning different from the other. An exception is made from a thing only when it is of the same kind or type in the action or the subject; when it is not so, there is no sense in making it an exception from it.

And His words: ﴿And Allah knows what you reveal﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: And Allah knows what you, O people, make apparent with your tongues of seeking permission when you seek permission to enter upon the occupants of inhabited houses, ﴿and what you conceal﴾, that is: and what you hide in your breasts when you do that, what it is that you intend by it: obedience to Allah and submission to His command, or something other than that.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 30:

The interpretation of His saying, ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.﴾ (24:30)

He, may He be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Say to the believing men﴾ in Allah and in you, O Muhammad, ﴿that they should lower their gaze﴾ means: that they should restrain their looking at what they desire to look at, of what Allah has forbidden them to look at. ﴿And guard their private parts﴾ from being seen by one who is not lawful for them to see, by wearing something that covers them from their eyes. ﴿That is purer for them﴾ means: for indeed, lowering their gaze from looking at what is not lawful to look at, and guarding the private parts from appearing to the eyes of onlookers, is purer for them with Allah and better. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do﴾ means: indeed Allah is possessed of knowledge of what you do, O people, in obeying Him regarding what He has commanded you concerning lowering your gaze from what He has commanded you to lower it from, and guarding your private parts from being exposed to one whom He has forbidden you to expose them to.

And the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said that:

Ali ibn Sahl al-Ramli narrated to me, he said: Hajjaj narrated to us, he said: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-'Aliyah, regarding His saying: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾, he said: Every private part whose guarding is mentioned in the Qur'an is from fornication, except this one: ﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾, for it means covering.

Ali narrated to me, he said: Abu Salih narrated to us, he said: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾ and ﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾, he said: That they lower their gaze from what Allah dislikes.

Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾, he said: Lowering one's gaze is not looking at what is unlawful for him; when he sees what is unlawful for him, he lowers his gaze so as not to look at it. No one can lower his entire gaze; Allah only said: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 24, Verse 31 (Part 1 of 2)**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts, and not display their adornment except what appears thereof, and let them draw their head-coverings over their chests, and not display their adornment except to their husbands, or their fathers, or their husbands' fathers, or their sons, or their husbands' sons, or their brothers, or their brothers' sons, or their sisters' sons, or their women, or what their right hands possess (31)﴾.

His exalted remembrance says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And say﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿to the believing women﴾ of your community, ﴿that they should lower their gaze﴾ from what Allah dislikes them to look at, of what He has forbidden you to look at. ﴿And guard their private parts﴾ means: and guard their private parts from being seen by anyone who is not permitted to see them, by wearing something that covers them from their eyes.

* *

And His words: ﴿and not display their adornment﴾.

His exalted remembrance says: and not reveal to people who are not their mahram (those with whom marriage is forbidden) their adornment. There are two kinds of adornment: the first is what is hidden, such as anklets, bracelets, earrings and necklaces. The second is what appears of it, and there is disagreement about what is meant by this in the verse. Some of them said: it is the outer garments.

Those who said this:

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, who said: Harun ibn al-Mughira narrated to us, from al-Hajjaj, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Adornment is of two kinds: what appears of it is the garments, and what is hidden is the two anklets, the two earrings and the two bracelets."
- Yunus narrated to me, who said: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: al-Thawri informed me, from Abu Ishaq al-Hamdani, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), that he said regarding ﴿except what appears thereof﴾: "It is the garments."
- Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, who said: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abd Allah, who said regarding ﴿except what appears thereof﴾: "The garments."
- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, who said: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, who said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abd Allah, similarly.
- He said: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Malik ibn al-Harith, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid, from Abd Allah, similarly.
- He said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Alqama, from Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i), regarding His words ﴿except what appears thereof﴾: "The garments."
- Ya'qub narrated to me, who said: Ibn Ulayya narrated to us, who said: one of our companions informed us, whether Yunus or someone else, from al-Hasan (al-Basri), regarding ﴿except what appears thereof﴾: "The garments."
- al-Hasan narrated to us, who said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, who said: Ma'mar informed us, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abd Allah, regarding ﴿except what appears thereof﴾: "The garments."

Abu Ishaq said: Do you not see that He said: ﴿Take your adornment at every place of worship﴾ (Q. 7:31)?

- al-Qasim narrated to us, who said: al-Husayn narrated to us, who said: Hajjaj narrated to me, who said: Muhammad ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Malik ibn al-Harith, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid, from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding ﴿except what appears thereof﴾: "It is the cloak."

Others said: What appears of the adornment that they are permitted to show is: kohl, the ring, the bracelets, and the face.

Those who said this:

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, who said: Marwan narrated to us, who said: Muslim al-Mala'i narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾: "Kohl and the ring."
- Amr ibn Abd al-Hamid al-Amuli narrated to us, who said: Marwan narrated to us, from Muslim al-Mala'i, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, similarly, but he did not mention Ibn Abbas.
- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, who said: Harun narrated to us, from Abu Abd Allah Nahshal, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "What appears of it is: kohl and the khiddan (the cheeks)."
- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, who said: Abu Asim narrated to us, who said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Hurmuz, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His words ﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾: "The face and the palm."
- Amr ibn Abd al-Hamid narrated to us, who said: Marwan ibn Mu'awiya narrated to us, from Abd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Hurmuz al-Makki, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, similarly.
- Ali ibn Sahl narrated to me, who said: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, who said: Abu Amr narrated to us, from Ata', regarding the words of Allah ﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾: "The two palms and the face."
- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, who said: Ibn Abi Adi narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada, who said: "Kohl, the two bracelets, and the ring."
- Ali narrated to me, who said: Abd Allah narrated to us, who said: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾. He said: "The adornment that appears is: the face, the kohl of the eye, the henna of the palm, and the ring. These are shown in her house to whoever enters upon her from among the people."
- al-Hasan narrated to us, who said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, who said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾: "The two bracelets, the ring and the kohl." Qatada said: "It has reached me that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to bare her hand except up to here,' and he gripped half of the forearm."
- al-Hasan narrated to us, who said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, who said: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Zuhri, from a man, from al-Miswar ibn Makhrama, regarding His words ﴿except what appears thereof﴾: "The two qulbs (bangles), the ring, and the kohl," meaning the bracelet.
- al-Qasim narrated to us, who said: al-Husayn narrated to us, who said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn Abbas said, regarding His words ﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾: "The ring and the maska (a bracelet)."

Ibn Jurayj said: Aisha said: "The qulb and the fatkha (a ring)." Aisha said: "My niece, the daughter of my maternal half-brother Abd Allah ibn al-Tufayl, came in to me adorned, and the Prophet (ﷺ) entered and turned away. Aisha said: 'O Messenger of Allah, she is my niece and a young girl.' He said: 'When a woman has menstruated [[ʿarakat al-jāriya ta'rak (from kanara) ʿarkan, ʿarākan and ʿurūkan: she menstruated; so she is ʿārik, and ʿa'rakat she is muʿrik]], it is not lawful for her to show anything except her face and what is beneath this,' and he gripped the forearm of himself, leaving between his grip and the palm the measure of another grip. Abu Ali pointed to this."

Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid said regarding His words ﴿except what appears thereof﴾: "Kohl, henna, and the ring."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, who said: Jarir narrated to us, from Asim, from Amir: regarding ﴿except what appears thereof﴾: "Kohl, henna, and the garments."
- Yunus narrated to me, who said: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾: "Of the adornment: kohl, henna and the ring. This is what they used to say, and this is what people see."
- Ibn Abd al-Rahim al-Barqi narrated to me, who said: Umar ibn Abi Salama narrated to us, who said: al-Awza'i was asked about ﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾, and he said: "The two palms and the face."
- Amr ibn Bundar narrated to us, who said: Marwan narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding His words ﴿and not display their adornment﴾: "The palm and the face."

Others said: it means the face and the garments.

Those who said this:

- Ibn Abd al-Ala narrated to us, who said: al-Mu'tamir narrated to us, who said: Yunus said: al-Hasan said regarding ﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾: "The face and the garments."
- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, who said: Ibn Abi Adi and Abd al-Ala narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada, from al-Hasan, regarding His words ﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾: "The face and the garments."

The most correct of these interpretations is the view of those who said: it means the face and the two palms, and what this includes is: kohl, the ring, the bracelet, and henna.

We said this is the most correct interpretation because of the consensus (ijma') of all that every worshipper must cover their nakedness ('awra) in prayer, that a woman may uncover her face and her palms in her prayer, and that she must cover what is other than that of her body. Except what has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he permitted her to show of her forearm up to the middle. Since this is agreed upon by all of them, it is known from this that she may show from her body what is not 'awra, just as that is permitted for men, because what is not 'awra is not forbidden to show. And since it is permitted for her to show that, it is known that it is among what Allah, exalted is His remembrance, excepted with His words ﴿except what appears thereof﴾, because all of that appears from her.

* *

And His words: ﴿and let them draw their head-coverings over their chests﴾. His exalted remembrance says: let them throw their khumur (head-coverings, the plural of khimar) over their chests (juyub), so that they cover with it their hair, their necks and their earrings.

- Ibn Waki' narrated to us, who said: Zayd ibn Hubab narrated to us, from Ibrahim ibn Nafi', who said: al-Hasan ibn Muslim ibn Yanaq narrated to us, from Safiyya bint Shayba, from Aisha, who said: "When this verse was revealed: ﴿and let them draw their head-coverings over their chests﴾, they tore the thick cloaks at the edges and covered themselves with them."
- Yunus narrated to me, who said: Ibn Wahb informed us, that Qurra ibn Abd al-Rahman informed him, from Ibn Shihab, from Urwa, from Aisha, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), that she said: "May Allah have mercy on the early emigrant women. When Allah revealed: ﴿and let them draw their head-coverings over their chests﴾, they tore their thickest murut (cloaks) and covered themselves with them."

* *

And His words: ﴿and not display their adornment except to their husbands﴾.

His exalted remembrance says: ﴿and not display their adornment﴾ which is not apparent, but rather what is hidden, and that is the anklet, the earring and the armlet, and what they were commanded to cover with their head-covering over the chest, and what is beyond what they are permitted to uncover and display in prayer and before non-mahram men, and the forearms up to above that, ﴿except to their husbands﴾.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said similarly to what we said about its interpretation.

Those who said this:

- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, who said: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, who said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur, from Talha ibn Musarrif, from Ibrahim, regarding ﴿and not display their adornment except to their husbands or their fathers﴾: "This is what is above the forearm."
- Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, who said: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Mansur, who said: I heard a man narrating from Talha, from Ibrahim, who said regarding this verse ﴿and not display their adornment except to their husbands, or their fathers, or their husbands' fathers﴾: "What is above the collar." Shu'ba said: "Mansur wrote it to me, and I read it to him."
- Ya'qub narrated to me, who said: Ibn Ulayya narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Arouba, from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿and not display their adornment except to their husbands﴾: "She may show the head to these."
- Ali narrated to me, who said: Abu Salih narrated to us, who said: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, who said: ﴿and not display their adornment except to their husbands﴾ ... up to His words ﴿the private parts of women﴾: "The adornment that they show to these is: their earrings, their necklace, and their bracelet. As for their anklets, their armbands, their necks and their hair, they show these only to their husbands."
- al-Qasim narrated to us, who said: al-Husayn narrated to us, who said: Hajjaj narrated to me, who said: Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn Mas'ud said, regarding His words ﴿and not display their adornment except to their husbands﴾: "The necklace and the two earrings." Allah, exalted is His remembrance, says: "Say to the believing free women: do not show this hidden adornment, which is not apparent, except to their husbands, who are their spouses (the singular being ba'l), or to their fathers, or to their husbands' fathers, meaning the fathers of their husbands, or to their sons, or to their husbands' sons, or to their brothers, or to their brothers' sons, or their sisters' sons, or their women." It was said: this refers to the women of the Muslims.

Those who said this:

- al-Qasim narrated to us, who said: al-Husayn narrated to us, who said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His words ﴿or their women﴾: "It has reached me that they are the women of the Muslims. It is not lawful for a Muslim woman to let a polytheist woman see her nakedness, except if she is a slave of hers. This is His words ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾."
- He said: al-Husayn narrated to me, who said: Isa ibn Yunus narrated to me, from Hisham ibn al-Ghazi, from Ubada ibn Nusay, that he disliked that a Muslim woman should accept a Christian woman, or let her see her nakedness, and he interpreted ﴿or their women﴾ accordingly.
- He said: Isa ibn Yunus narrated to us, from Hisham, from Ubada, who said: "Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, may Allah have mercy on them both: 'To proceed: it has reached me that women enter the bathhouses with them women of the People of the Book. Prohibit this and prevent it.'" He said: "Then Abu Ubayda stood up in that place, supplicating: 'O Allah, any woman who enters the bathhouse without illness or sickness, seeking whiteness for her face, let her face be blackened on the day when faces turn white.'"

And regarding His words ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾, the people of interpretation differed about its meaning. Some of them said: "Or their male slaves (mamalik), for there is no harm in her showing them of her adornment what she shows to these."

Those who said this:

- al-Qasim narrated to us, who said: al-Husayn narrated to us, who said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Amr ibn Dinar informed me, from Mikhlad al-Tamimi, that he said regarding His words ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾: "In the first reading: 'your right hands' (aymanukum)."

Others said: rather, the meaning is: "or what their right hands possess of the slave women of the polytheists," as we have already mentioned from Ibn Jurayj earlier, that when he said ﴿or their women﴾ he meant the Muslim women and not the polytheist women, and then he said: "or what their right hands possess of the polytheist slave women."

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿or male attendants who have no desire, or children who have not yet attained knowledge of women's private parts. And let them not stamp their feet so that what they hide of their adornment may be known. And turn to Allah in repentance all together, O believers, that you may succeed (31)﴾.

His exalted remembrance says: ﴿those who follow you for food that they eat at your place, of men who have no need of women, and no desire for them.﴾

The people of interpretation said similarly to what we said about this.

Those who said this:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, who said: my father narrated to me, who said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, who said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿or male attendants who have no desire﴾: "A man used to follow a man in the earlier times, and he was not jealous over him, and the woman did not fear to take off her head-covering in his presence. He is the fool who has no need of women."
- Ali narrated to me, who said: Abu Salih narrated to us, who said: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿or male attendants who have no desire﴾: "This is the man who follows the people, and he is dull-witted in his mind, who is not concerned with women and does not desire them. The adornment that she shows to these is her earrings, her necklace, and her bracelets. As for her anklets, her armbands, her neck and her hair, she shows these only to her husband."
- al-Hasan narrated to us, who said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, who said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿or male attendants﴾: "He is the attendant who follows you and eats some of your food."
- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, who said: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, who said: Isma'il ibn Ulayya narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿or male attendants who have no desire﴾: "He is the one who wants food and does not want women."
- He said: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, who said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.
- Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, who said: Abu Asim narrated to us, who said: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, who said: al-Hasan narrated to us, who said: Warqa narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿or male attendants who have no desire﴾: "Those whose concern is only their bellies, and who are not feared with regard to women."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 31 (part 2 of 2):

⁕ Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the like of it.

⁕ Isma'il ibn Musa al-Suddi narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿other than those men who have no physical desire﴾, he said: the imbecile (al-ablah).

⁕ Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: I heard Layth, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿other than those men who have no physical desire﴾, he said: He is the imbecile (al-ablah) who does not recognize anything about women.

⁕ Ya'qub related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Najih narrated to us, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿other than those men who have no physical desire among the men﴾, he said: one who has no desire for women, such as so-and-so.

⁕ Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn 'Atiyyah narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from one who narrated to him, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿other than those men who have no physical desire﴾, he said: He is the one from whom women feel no shame.

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mughirah, from al-Sha'bi: ﴿other than those men who have no physical desire﴾, he said: the one who follows a man and his household, who has not reached the point of desire to look upon the nakedness of women.

⁕ Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Shu'bah, from al-Mughirah, from al-Sha'bi, ﴿other than those men who have no physical desire﴾, he said: the one who has no desire for women.

⁕ He said: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: the mentally deficient (al-mu'tuh).

⁕ al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri regarding His words: ﴿or the male attendants who have no physical desire among the men﴾, he said: He is the fool (al-ahmaq) who has no ambition for women and no desire.
And with this chain, from Ma'mar, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, regarding His words: ﴿other than those men who have no physical desire among the men﴾, he says: the fool (al-ahmaq) who has no inclination toward women.

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: the one who has no need of women.

⁕ Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿or the male attendants who have no physical desire among the men﴾, he said: He is the one who follows a people so closely that it is as if he were one of them and grew up among them, and he follows them not out of desire for their women, and has no desire for their women; rather, he follows them for the provision they give him.

⁕ al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Zuhri, from 'Urwah, from 'A'ishah, who said: A man called a mukhannath (effeminate man) used to enter upon the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, and they considered him among those who have no physical desire. One day the Prophet ﷺ entered upon him while he was with some of his wives, and he was describing a woman, saying: "When she comes forward, she comes with four (folds), and when she turns away, she turns away with eight." The Prophet ﷺ said: "I do not think this one knows what is here; let this one not enter upon you." So they veiled him from them.

⁕ Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam al-Misri related to me, saying: Hafs ibn 'Umar al-'Adani narrated to us, saying: al-Hakam ibn Aban narrated to us, from 'Ikrimah regarding His words: ﴿or the male attendants who have no physical desire﴾, he said: He is the mukhannath whose penis does not stand erect.

The reciters differed regarding His words: ﴿ghayri ulil-irbah﴾. Some of the people of Syria, and some of the people of Madinah and Kufah, recited it as "ghayra ulil-irbah" with ghayr in the accusative. The accusative of ghayr here has two possible grounds: first, as a qat' (a shift to a separate status) from "al-tabi'in," since al-tabi'in is definite while ghayr is indefinite; and second, as an istithna' (exception), treating ghayr as having the meaning of "illa" (except), so that it is as if it were said: "illa." Others among those I have mentioned recited ghayr with a genitive, "ghayri," making it a description (na't) of al-tabi'in, and the description of al-tabi'in by "ghayr" is permissible even though al-tabi'in is definite and ghayr is indefinite, because al-tabi'in is a definite that is not specified by time. The interpretation of the statement according to this reading is: "or those whose description is this."

My view on this is that they are two readings close in meaning, both widely transmitted in the cities, so whichever one the reciter reads is correct. However, the genitive in "ghayr" is stronger in Arabic, so reciting with it is more pleasing to me. Al-irbah (الإربة) is the form of the verbal noun from al-arab, like al-jilsah from al-julus and al-mishyah from al-mashy, and it means need, as one says: "la arba li fika" (I have no need of you), meaning "la hajata li fika" (I have no need for you); similarly, "aribtu li kadha wa kadha" means: I needed it, so I am ara lahu arban. As for al-urbah with a damma on the alif, it means the knot.

* *

His words: ﴿or the children who have not yet attained knowledge of the private parts of women﴾
He, exalted is His remembrance, says: or the children who have not uncovered the nakedness of women through intercourse with them, such that they gain knowledge of them due to their young age.
The people of interpretation have said similarly to what we have said.
Those who said this:

⁕ Muhammad related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿upon the nakedness of women﴾, he said: they do not know what is there, due to their youth before puberty.

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* *

His words: ﴿And let them not stamp their feet so that what they hide of their adornment may be known﴾
He, exalted is His remembrance, says: and let them not put on their feet any of the ornaments which, when they walk or move them, make known to the people among whom they walk what they hide of such things.
The people of interpretation have said similarly to what we have said.
Those who said this:

⁕ Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir narrated to us, from his father, who said: A Hadrami claimed that a woman took two bura (plural of burah, meaning every ring of a bracelet, earring, anklet and the like) of silver, and took a jaz' (a kind of stone or bead), then passed by a group of people and stamped with her foot, so the anklet struck the bead and it made a sound. So Allah revealed: ﴿And let them not stamp their feet so that what they hide of their adornment may be known﴾.

⁕ Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik: ﴿And let them not stamp their feet so that what they hide of their adornment may be known﴾, he said: their feet had beads, so when they passed by gatherings they moved their feet so that what they hid of their adornment would be known.

⁕ 'Ali related to me, saying: 'Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And let them not stamp their feet﴾, it means that one strikes one anklet against another in front of men, and she has anklets on her feet, and she moves them in front of men; so Allah, glorified and exalted, forbade that, because it is from the work of Satan.

⁕ al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah: ﴿And let them not stamp their feet so that what they hide of their adornment may be known﴾, he said: it is the anklet; a woman should not strike her foot so that the sound of her anklet is heard.

⁕ Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿And let them not stamp their feet so that what they hide of their adornment may be known﴾, he said: the bells among their ornaments, which they put on their feet in place of anklets, so Allah forbade them from stamping their feet so that those bells would be heard.

* *

His words: ﴿And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers﴾
